extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students (practitioners and scholars of U.S. patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing patent disclaimers and reissued patents in U.S. law: when a disclaimer or reissue is available, formal requirements, timing and delay consequences (including costs), limits on scope, effects on litigation, and the conditions for reissue (same invention, surrender, new specification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of inadvertent overclaiming
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, and without any fraudulent or deceptive intention, a patentee has in his specification claimed materially more than that of which he was the first inventor, his patent shall be valid for whatever is justly his own; and every such patentee ... may maintain a suit ... for the infringement of such part, if it is a material and substantial part of the thing patented, and is definitely distinguishable from the parts claimed without right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim(s) cover more than the patentee's invention due to innocent error, the statute preserves rights in the true invention but only to the material/substantial and definitely distinguishable part. The patentee must take appropriate steps (disclaimer) to avoid statutory consequences; otherwise limitations apply (see costs/unreasonable delay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to enter disclaimer to recover costs
rubrics_metrics.description: In every such case, in which a judgment or decree shall be rendered for the plaintiff, no costs shall be recovered, unless the proper disclaimer was entered in the Patent Office, before the commencement of the suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plaintiff who later proves some claims invalid/overbroad cannot obtain costs unless the proper disclaimer was filed at the Patent Office before suit began. This is strict and applies even if the delay in filing the disclaimer was not unreasonable in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bar for unreasonable neglect or delay in filing disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: No patentee shall be entitled to maintain any such suit, if he has unreasonably neglected or delayed to enter a disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether delay is 'unreasonable' is a mixed question of law and fact for the jury/court and depends on when knowledge of the need to disclaim was brought home and on surrounding circumstances; reasonable dispute about necessity suspends the running of delay until resolved by courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalities of a disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: Any such patentee ... may, on payment of the fee required by law, make disclaimer of such parts of the subject-matter of the patent, as he shall not choose to longer claim, stating therein the extent of his interest in such patent. Such disclaimer shall be in writing, attested by one or more witnesses, and recorded in the Patent Office, and shall thereafter be considered a part of the original specification to the extent of the interest possessed by the disclaimant and by those claiming under him after the record thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaimers must be written, witnessed, recorded, and state the disclaimant's interest; once recorded they are treated as part of the specification to the stated extent. If the disclaimant is the original patentee and the disclaimer is silent on transfers, it fairly implies full ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of errors that justify disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Such errors may spring from inadvertence. ... So also, they may arise from accident: from chances against which even diligent care cannot always guard. But mistake is the most common source of such errors; and such errors may arise from mistake of fact or from mistake of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaimers are intended to remedy innocent errors (inadvertence, accident, mistake of fact or law). Fraudulent or deceptive intention precludes relief by disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake of fact — prior art disclosure and reasonable time to disclaim
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistakes of fact, relative to how much of a described process, machine or manufacture was first invented by its patentee, frequently follow from lack of full information touching what was previously invented by others. ... the statute provides that he must disclaim that part, within a reasonable time, or, in default thereof, must suffer the statutory consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When subsequent information (e.g., litigation) shows prior invention by others, the patentee should disclaim the prior subject-matter within a reasonable time to preserve rights in the residue; 'reasonable time' depends on when knowledge is imputed to the patentee and whether a bona fide dispute exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer cannot create a new ground not in the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: But a disclaimer cannot confine a claim to ground which does not appear in the patent to constitute an invention; even where that ground is narrower than that which was originally claimed in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer cannot be used to reformulate or invent a new basis of patentability that is not supported by the original patent; it can only carve away matter from what was claimed or clarify boundaries that appear in the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake of law — disclaimer of unpatentable subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A mistake of law, which consists in claiming something not patentable, may also be remedied by disclaimer. The law which permits a patentee to disclaim, is remedial. ... The same reason would also permit a patentee to disclaim any claim which is void for want of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is held void for lack of patentability (invention), the patentee may disclaim that claim to preserve the remainder; statutory remedy applies similarly whether void for lack of novelty or lack of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers for multiple independent inventions (unity defects)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mistake of law, which consisted in unlawfully claiming, in separate claims, in one patent, several independent inventions, may be remedied by disclaiming enough claims to give to the patent the necessary unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If separate independent inventions were improperly claimed together, selective disclaimers can be used to restore unity by removing some independent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: No disclaimer available for want of utility
rubrics_metrics.description: There appears to be no warrant in the statute, for disclaiming any claim which is void for want of utility, and for no other cause. ... If a patent has but one claim, and where the matter covered by that claim is useless, no disclaimer could make that patent valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility defects cannot generally be cured by disclaimer. If only certain claims are useless but others valid, the useless claims are not injurious to valid ones and disclaimer is unnecessary; disclaimer cannot resurrect a wholly useless single-claim patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: No disclaimer necessary for claims void by constructive abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: And no disclaimer is necessary where some, but not all, of the claims of a patent are void, by reason of constructive abandonment, resulting from public use or sale of the subjects of those particular claims, more than two years prior to the application for the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims invalidated by prior public use/sale (more than two years pre-application) need not be disclaimed because they do not injure the valid claims; disclaimer statutes do not apply to such constructive abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a disclaimer must leave a material distinguishable part
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute provides that a disclaimer, to be effective, must leave claimed by the patent, at least one definitely distinguishable and material part of the original subject of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer cannot eliminate all meaningful scope; it must preserve at least one material and definitely distinguishable part of the original subject-matter (commonly done by disclaiming some claims while leaving independent ones untouched).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaiming parts within a single claim (phrasing with 'or' or 'with or without')
rubrics_metrics.description: For example, where two or more claims in substance, are combined in one claim in form, by the use of the words 'with or without' or by use of the word 'or' alone, a disclaimer may be made to expunge one of those inventions from that claim, without disturbing any other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a single claim in form covers alternative inventions, the patentee can disclaim one alternative to narrow the claim without disturbing others — i.e., disaggregate alternatives phrased in the claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaim generic claim while preserving specific claim
rubrics_metrics.description: And where a patent contains a proper specific claim, and also a generic claim which covers not only the subject of the specific claim, but also covers other matter which requires to be disclaimed, that result can be accomplished by a disclaimer of the generic claim, without any injury resulting to the specific claim, from that disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaiming a broad/generic claim is an appropriate way to excise overbroad scope while leaving narrower, specific claims intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use disclaimer to confine claim construction to boundaries of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: And where an invention is limited by the prior art, in some particular in which the patent states that it is not limited, that statement may be removed by a disclaimer, so as to confine the construction of the claim of the patent, to the boundaries to which the invention is limited by the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer can remove statements in the patent that falsely assert non-limitation, thereby aligning claim construction with the true limits imposed by prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot disclaim surplus parts of combination and then accuse others of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the invention of a patentee consisted in a combination of less than all of the parts specified in a combination claim in his patent, he cannot disclaim the surplus parts, and afterward hold as infringers, those who make, use or sell the other parts alone, ... because that operation would broaden the patent instead of narrowing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaimers must not be used to impermissibly broaden claim scope by shedding elements and then asserting the remaining elements as infringed; that would defeat the statutory purpose of narrowing, not broadening, monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions shown only in drawings but not claimed cannot be monopolized by disclaiming others
rubrics_metrics.description: And where the only invention left to a patentee by the prior art, is shown in the drawings of his patent, but is not mentioned in the description, or attended to in any claim of that document; that invention is not such a part of the subject of the patent, as can be monopolized by disclaiming all that the patent described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unclaimed invention merely depicted in drawings but not described/claimed cannot be converted into claimable subject-matter via disclaimer of other things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers unavailable for fraudulently obtained overclaims
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraudulent or deceptive intention, if it existed on the part of a patentee, when claiming materially more than that of which he was the first inventor, or when claiming that which was not patentable, will rightly prevent him from receiving any benefit from a disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory remedial scheme applies only to innocent errors; intentional misconduct or fraud bars relief by disclaimer as a matter of equity and statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of neglect/delay begins with knowledge; reasonable doubt suspends it
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglect or delay to file a necessary disclaimer, begins when knowledge is brought home to the patentee, that the inventor upon whose account the patent was granted, was not the first inventor of a particular thing claimed in the patent, and material to the subject of the patent as a whole. If, however, there is reasonable ground for difference of opinion relevant to the question whether the prior patent ... really negatives the novelty of anything claimed by him, then unreasonable delay to file a disclaimer will not begin until that question is finally settled by the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'clock' for unreasonable delay runs from imputed knowledge; but bona fide, reasonable disputes about novelty/inventorship suspend the start until judicial resolution. Short further delays after resolution are sometimes excused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent expiration prevents filing or necessity of disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent has expired when the occasion for a disclaimer is established, no disclaimer can be filed or is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the patent term has expired there is no mechanism/no need to file a disclaimer under these statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences on costs when disclaimer filed pending or after suit
rubrics_metrics.description: No costs can be recovered by the plaintiff in any infringement suit, the final decision of which shows a necessity for a disclaimer, unless such a disclaimer was entered in the Patent Office before the commencement of the suit. This rule applies even to cases where the delay to enter the disclaimer was not unreasonable. But a verdict on all the claims of a patent entitles the plaintiff to costs, even if, after that verdict, he files a disclaimer to one or more of the claims of that patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a disclaimer after suit begins generally prevents recovery of costs if the final decision shows a disclaimer was necessary; however if the plaintiff wins on all claims (verdict), he may still obtain costs despite later disclaimers. Filing a disclaimer during suit does not itself affect the pending action except as to whether delay was unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content sufficiency and effect of disclaimers by different parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclaimers are required to state the extent of the interest which is held by the disclaimant in the patent involved. If, however, the disclaimant is the original patentee, and the disclaimer states that fact, and is silent respecting any transfer of any part of it, the fair implication is that he still owns the whole, and that implication is a sufficient statement of the interest of the patentee. But if only one of several joint owners or owners in common of a patent, should file a disclaimer, no other owner could avail himself of its benefits, nor could it affect a suit brought by all the owners jointly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer must adequately state the disclaimant's interest; certain presumptions suffice for original patentees or executors/administrators, but disclaimers by only some co-owners do not bind or benefit non-filing co-owners or joint suits by all owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of patent after disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of a patent, after a disclaimer has been properly entered, must be the same that it would have been if the matter so disclaimed had never been claimed. The mere fact of disclaimer is no evidence that the matter disclaimed is a part of the prior art. And where a disclaimer disclaims a particular thing specifically, that thing cannot afterward be covered by the patent as being an equivalent of another thing which was not disclaimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must construe the disclaimed patent as if the disclaimed matter had never been claimed; disclaimers do not operate as admissions that matter is prior art and bar later claims that the disclaimed thing is an equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing disclaimers pending suit or appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclaimers may be filed pending a suit on the patent, even though an appeal has been had; but the plaintiff, even if he prevails in the suit, can recover no costs. The filing of a disclaimer at that stage of affairs does not affect the pending action; except so far as it may bear upon the question whether or not there was unreasonable delay before filing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a disclaimer during litigation or appeal is permitted and often wise to minimize the risk of being held to have unreasonably delayed; it does not otherwise change procedural posture except for the delay/costs issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial practice varies on whether decree should await disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a District Court, before any disclaimer has been filed, decides that a part of the claims ... are valid, and have been infringed ... while another part are void ... and ought therefore to be disclaimed. Ought the judge ... to enter a decree for an injunction and an account on the valid claims, and allow the complainant to disclaim the others ...; or should he decline to enter any decree till the complainant shall have filed a disclaimer? The second of these courses has been the practice in the first circuit, in the sixth, and prior to Page Machine Co. v. Dow, in the second; other circuits have taken different approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circuit courts differ: some require the complainant to file a disclaimer before a decree; others allow decrees on valid claims and permit the complainant to disclaim later. Practitioners should be aware of circuit-specific practice and plan accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue available to correct defects caused by inadvertence, accident, or mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever any patent should be inoperative or invalid because the inventor had, by inadvertence, accident, or mistake, and without any fraudulent or deceptive intention, made his description or specification defective or insufficient, ... it should be lawful ... to cause a new patent to be granted to the same inventor, for the same invention, and for the residue of the term of the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissues are statutory relief to correct defective/insufficient specifications or other inadvertent faults; reissue requires surrender of the original patent and delivery of a sufficient specification and is limited to the same invention and the remaining term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissues extend to executors, administrators, and assigns; reissue patents subject to same defenses and do not lose post-grant infringement recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: That statute also provided, in effect, that the right to receive a reissue, should extend to executors, administrators or assigns; and that the reissue patent should be liable to the same defences as the original; and that no public use of the invention, after the grant of the original patent, should prejudice the right of the patentee to recover for infringement of the reissue patent, committed after the grant thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue rights are transferable and the reissued patent stands subject to the same defenses as the original; public use after the original grant does not bar recovery for infringement occurring after reissue (per the statute as described).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner authority to cancel and reissue on Patent Office error or inventor's mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: In pursuance of the doctrines of Grant v. Raymond, the Commissioner may cancel a patent and issue a corrected one in its stead, where the first one was caused, by an inadvertent error in the Patent Office, to grant less to the inventor than he had applied for and was entitled to receive, and where the inventor refuses to accept the patent thus limited. And it was ... that the Commissioner of Patents once reissued a patent to correct an error in its drawing, without making any change in specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Patent Office has historical authority to reissue to correct errors including Office errors and drawing errors; reissue relief may sometimes be available even when statute does not expressly provide, but modern practice follows statutory requisites (surrender, new specification, same invention).
